Internal: the shape of a CSV file, checked before it is read

Source: R/io.R
dot-jst_csv_check_shape.Rd

read.csv() decides how many variables a file has from its first line and its first five lines, and two shapes go wrong without a word (the import audit, Session 362): a first line with FEWER fields than the lines below it – a title above the names, a missing name, a semicolon file from European Excel – makes the first values of every line row names, which jload() then drops, or stops on R's "more columns than column names"; and a line further down with MORE fields than the first is split into two cases. Every line's fields are counted first (count.fields(), quoting as read.csv() quotes), and those shapes stop here, saying what the file holds and what to do. A line with fewer fields than the first is read as it always was, its last cells empty.

Usage

.jst_csv_check_shape(path, skip, enc, shown, line_for, obj_name, header = TRUE)

Arguments

path

The file.

skip

Lines skipped above the names.

enc

NULL, or the encoding the file is read in.

shown

The file's name for the prose.

line_for

jload()'s line builder: line_for(skip = 2) gives the jload() call that reads the file with skip = 2.

obj_name

The data frame's name, for the read.csv2() line.

header

As jload() reads the file.

Value

Invisibly: with header = FALSE the number of values most lines hold (NULL when the lines could not be counted); otherwise NULL. Or stops.

Details

Read with header = FALSE (ruling R21, Session 365) a file has no names line to measure the others against: every line is a case, measured against the count most lines hold. A line holding more stops, as a line longer than the names line does; a shorter one is read with its last cells empty; the title search, which looks for a names line, is not made. The count is returned, and jload() reads that many variables (col.names), so a long line past the first five – the lines read.csv() counts – could not be split even if one got through.
